name: Weekly Executive Update
description: How the weekly executive update is produced and how to think about it: read that week's notes from the four standing weekly meetings, think across them by area, and write one briefing in the shape of the project's template that runs the 30-minute executive sync.
narrative:
The weekly executive update is the single briefing that runs the company's 30-minute weekly executive sync. Its reader is leadership walking into that meeting, and its job is to make the meeting work: decide, unblock, align. It is not a recap of four meetings. Build it only from the four standing weekly meetings — the Weekly Sync, Client Projects + Maintenance, Platform Weekly, and the Operations Sync — and never from any other meeting (the Weekly Strategy Meeting, the Board meeting), even if its notes are shared with the agent too.

Gather the notes from Google Drive, never from the calendar — the calendar shows a meeting, not its notes. Each designated meeting is a resource of the project this work runs in, named exactly as Google names that meeting's notes. The agent is an invitee of every designated meeting, so after each occurrence Google shares that occurrence's transcript with it directly: a Google Doc owned by the host, named for the meeting, its date and time, and 'Transcript'. Those files sit in the host's own 'Google Meet' folders, which Google re-creates whenever one is shared — so never look for notes through a folder; find each meeting's notes by its name among the files shared with the agent. Read the transcript document, never the recording video; if an occurrence has no transcript but has 'Notes by Gemini', those notes will do.

Use only this week's notes: those created since last week's briefing was written, exactly a week ago. That is normally one occurrence per meeting, and a transcript that landed just after last week's briefing belongs to this week's. Never fold in an older week — last week's briefing already covered it. If a designated meeting has nothing new — it was skipped, or it met this morning and its transcript has not landed yet — say so in one line with the date of its newest notes, and brief the rest. If none of the four has anything new, do not produce a briefing: report what was searched and the newest notes found for each, so the operator can see whether the meetings were held and whether their notes are reaching the agent.

How to think about it. Read all four sets of notes before writing a word, then think across them: the same client, project or problem usually comes up in more than one meeting, and the briefing should say it once, in its area, with its latest state. Write by area, never meeting by meeting. Hold every line to one test — so what? A line earns its place when it tells leadership what changed, what is at risk, or what they need to decide; routine updates and chatter roll up into a line or drop out, and a twenty-row action dump is a transcription, not a briefing. Prefer the specific to the general: the client, the number, the date, the person. Tie each point to the meeting it came from. Where the notes are unclear or disagree, say so rather than smoothing it over, and never invent an owner, a due date or a decision the notes do not contain — "not set" is an honest answer.

The shape is the project's briefing template — a document the operator edits — so read it every time instead of working from memory. It fixes the sections, their order and what goes in each; its bracketed lines are guidance to replace, never text to copy. Every proper name and term goes through the project's names and terms before it reaches the page: transcripts mishear names, and a briefing that misspells a client or the company's own product loses the room. The company's product is peregrine3 — lowercase, one word — however a transcript renders it ("Paragrin 3", "Paragon 3"); likewise TEFCA, SOC 2, HCSC, BCBSM, Elevance, Wellstar. A name you cannot confirm stays as the transcript has it, flagged in the notes.

Produce exactly ONE document for the week, in a single pass: write the whole briefing and create the branded Google Doc in the same step, applying the exec-brief brand reference (a resource of the project) as you create it, so nothing is lost between hand-offs. The document title is added when it is created — do not repeat it inside the briefing. If one for this week already exists in the Weekly Exec Summaries folder, move it to the trash and create the briefing fresh, so exactly one remains — creating is the path that carries the whole structure. Place it in the Weekly Exec Summaries folder and leave its sharing alone: it inherits the folder's access, which is exactly who should read it.

Then close the loop with evidence: read the finished document back, confirm every section of the template is there in order with real content, and report its link and the notes it was built from, each with its date. Report only what you actually did — a step you did not take does not go in the report. That read-back IS the proof the work is done; a claim that the document was created, without reading it back to show its content, is not enough and will not verify.
